Neonatal body mass of the Eurasian water shrew Neomys fodiens is remarkably low, with newborns weighing approximately 0.78 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.78 grams] at birth. This modest size is typical for altricial insectivores and places the species among the smallest neonatal soricids. Lactation proceeds rapidly under the species' elevated body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], a thermal regime that accelerates early development. The time since birth at weaning is 32 days [tx = 32 days], after which the young transition to independent foraging at a temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This relatively brief suckling period is facilitated by the mother's high metabolic output and the calorically dense milk characteristic of shrews. Observations from captive colonies indicate that weanlings begin capturing small aquatic invertebrates almost immediately after nutritional independence is achieved, reflecting the strong selective pressure to exploit productive riparian habitats during the short northern summer.

At a maternal body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], gestation in the Eurasian water shrew lasts for 20 days [tg = 20 days], a duration that aligns closely with predictions for mammals of this size class. The high metabolic rate demanded by endothermy imposes a significant energetic burden on gravid females, which may account for the relatively small litter sizes compared to other shrew species. Embryogenesis proceeds through rapid organogenesis in utero, and parturition typically yields three to eight altricial neonates. The brevity of gestation implies that a substantial portion of foetal growth occurs during the final days of pregnancy, placing a premium on the mother's ability to sustain elevated food intake. Field studies have noted that females occupy territories with dense ground cover and abundant prey during the breeding season, likely as an adaptive response to the high metabolic costs of gestation.

Juveniles reach sexual maturity at 106 days since birth [tp = 106 days since birth], a developmental schedule that permits reproduction within the same calendar year for early-born litters at a temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This rapid maturation is supported by the species' sustained high body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], which elevates basal metabolic rates and accelerates tissue growth. The onset of puberty is accompanied by gonadal activation, and histological examination of captive individuals reveals spermatogenesis in males and follicular development in females shortly after this milestone. Shrews that mature later in the season typically delay their first breeding attempt until the following spring, suggesting a photoperiodic modulation of reproductive readiness. The relatively short time to maturity is a common life-history trait among small-bodied insectivores inhabiting temperate zones with brief windows of prey abundance.

Maximum lifespan in the Eurasian water shrew has been recorded at approximately 3.1 years [am = approximately 3.1 years] when individuals are maintained under the thermal conditions typical of their active metabolic state (37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]). This longevity is remarkably high for a mammal of such diminutive size, as most soricids of comparable body mass rarely exceed two years in the wild. The extended lifespan may be linked to the species' semi-aquatic foraging niche, which reduces predation risk and provides access to a relatively stable year-round food supply of aquatic invertebrates. Senescence manifests gradually, with older individuals showing reduced dentition and diminished hunting efficiency. Notably, captive animals have been documented to survive beyond this figure, but field records consistently place the upper boundary of natural mortality at approximately 1,131 days post-birth.

Adult body mass in this species reaches an ultimate wet weight of 16 grams [Wwi = 16 grams], a value consistent with the range of 15 to 19 grams reported in field guides. This asymptotic mass is attained after the completion of skeletal growth, usually within the first few months following weaning (which occurs at a wet weight at weaning of 10 grams [Wwx = 10 grams]). This post-weaning mass gain of approximately 6 grams is among the most rapid recorded in small soricids and highlights the energetic surplus available in productive riparian habitats. Captive feeding trials have shown that sub-adults can double their body mass in just three weeks when provided with unlimited prey. Under the standard thermal regime of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], females typically produce 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5 pups per litter] and raise approximately 1.8 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.8 litters per year], a figure that aligns with calculated rates for other Neomys species and underscores the energetic limits imposed by small body size and endothermy.
